question.:question/problem:
Consider the following system of equations.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y &=1 - 2x \\ y &=-2x + 1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

The lines corresponding to the equations {{field-1}}. Therefore, the system has {{field-2}}, meaning that it's {{field-3}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
A system of equations is *consistent* if it has at least one solution. Otherwise, it is called *inconsistent*.

Consistent systems, in turn, can be of the following two types:

- When a system of equations has a *single* solution, it is called *consistent independent*.
- When a system of equations has an *infinite number* of solutions, it is called *consistent dependent*.

We can summarize these definitions using the diagram shown below.

![](images/16/1692fbea298339ff839cf2f14986d51af45d1ec72b2b7d0de179336bdef40c0e.png)

The solutions of a linear system with two variables correspond to the points of intersection of the two lines defined by the equations. Three possibilities exist, as shown below.

![](images/8c/8c544df38ce82dd70c3d01718233c9fae1fae0534748892643a12b6556918fb7.png)

Notice that the equations in the system have the same slopes ($-2$) and the same $y$-intercepts ($1$). So, the lines $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{coincide with each other}}$ and share every point.

Therefore, the system has $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{infinitely many solutions}}$, meaning that it's $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{consistent dependent}}$.

Consistent systems, in turn, can be of the following two types:

- When a system of equations has a *single* solution, it is called *consistent independent*.
- When a system of equations has an *infinite number* of solutions, it is called *consistent dependent*.

We can summarize these definitions using the diagram shown below.

![](images/16/1692fbea298339ff839cf2f14986d51af45d1ec72b2b7d0de179336bdef40c0e.png)

The solutions of a linear system with two variables correspond to the points of intersection of the two lines defined by the equations. Three possibilities exist, as shown below.

![](images/8c/8c544df38ce82dd70c3d01718233c9fae1fae0534748892643a12b6556918fb7.png)

Notice that the equations in the system have the same slopes ($-6$) and the same $y$-intercepts ($5$). So, the lines $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{coincide with each other}}$ and share every point.

Therefore, the system has $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{infinitely many solutions}}$, meaning that it's $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{consistent dependent}}$.

Consider the following system of equations.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y &=2 - 3x \\ y &=-3x + 2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

The lines corresponding to the equations {{field-1}}. Therefore, the system has {{field-2}}, meaning that it's {{field-3}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
A system of equations is *consistent* if it has at least one solution. Otherwise, it is called *inconsistent*.

Consistent systems, in turn, can be of the following two types:

- When a system of equations has a *single* solution, it is called *consistent independent*.
- When a system of equations has an *infinite number* of solutions, it is called *consistent dependent*.

We can summarize these definitions using the diagram shown below.

![](images/16/1692fbea298339ff839cf2f14986d51af45d1ec72b2b7d0de179336bdef40c0e.png)

The solutions of a linear system with two variables correspond to the points of intersection of the two lines defined by the equations. Three possibilities exist, as shown below.

![](images/8c/8c544df38ce82dd70c3d01718233c9fae1fae0534748892643a12b6556918fb7.png)

Notice that the equations in the system have the same slopes ($-3$) and the same $y$-intercepts ($2$). So, the lines $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{coincide with each other}}$ and share every point.

Therefore, the system has $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{infinitely many solutions}}$, meaning that it's $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{consistent dependent}}$.
